title.narrative: Improving the Recognition and Land Regularization of Brazilian Quilombola (Slave Descendent) Communities

description.narrative: The Ministry of Education, in collaboration with the Ministry of Culture , is requested IDF financing for institutional strengthening of Funda ção Cultural Palmares (FCP) which in 1999 was assigned the lead agency responsibility in Brazil for recognizing and regularizing the lands of the quilombola or descendents of escaped slave communities that were formed from the 17th century until 1888 when slavery was abolished in Brazil . It is estimated that there are approximately 1000 such communities with an average population of 100 persons each in 15 states, primarily in the Northeast. These communities are among the poorest of the rural poor in Brazil. Regularization of their lands is one of their highest priorities and is clearly fundamental to protecting their way of life and improving their social and economic well-being. Twelve years ago, the nation-state acknowledged the quilombolas and their quest for land regularization in Article 68 of the 1988 Constitution that indicates that the Government should provide land titles to remaining members of quilombola communities. However, in the ensuring years very few quilombo land regularizations have occurred and the legal and regulatory framework for carrying them out is still quite weak and ambiguous. The FCP was also created in 1988, however, its original legal mandate was to help protect and preserve Afro-B razilian cultural heritage in general. Meanwhile the Agrarian Reform Institute (INCRA) and several states carried out some efforts toward quilombo land regularization with mixed success and relatively little formalization or institutionalization of processes and procedures. In 1999, the lead responsibility for carrying out Article 68 of the Constitution was transferred to FCP, an agency with considerable familarityfamiliarity with quilombola issues, but no track record or experience in dealing with the complexities of land regularization. Furthermore, a number of legal issues (detailed below) remain pending. Therefore, the IDF grant will finance: I) Improving the Legal Framework for Recognition and Land Regularization; II) Institutional Assessment and Strengthening of FCP and Partnerships; III) Establishing a National Database on I dentified and To B e Identified Quilombola Communities in Brazil; and IV) Capacity-Building and Pilot Land Regularizations.
